source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note); Lowell Offering and Dickens wording verified against the Project Gutenberg texts; O'Sullivan wording verified against Wikisource
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the market revolution changed the lives of American workers in the period 1800-1848.

documents.title: The Lowell mills open
documents.source: Account of the opening of the Lowell mills, 1823, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the new textile mills at Lowell, Massachusetts, and the workers they hired.
documents.text: In 1823, textile mills opened at Lowell, Massachusetts, along the Merrimack River. The mills hired young women from New England farm families, housed them in supervised company boardinghouses, and paid them cash wages for a few years of work before they returned home to marry.

documents.title: The mill women strike
documents.source: Account of the Lowell turn-out of 1834, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A description of the mill women's turn-outs, written from the workers' side.
documents.text: In 1834, the mill women of Lowell staged a turn-out to protest a cut in their wages. The strike failed, but two years later the women organized as the Factory Girls Association and had greater success protesting a rent increase in the company boardinghouses.

documents.title: A nation of many nations
documents.source: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, November 1839. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A journalist's celebration of America as a nation built by immigrants from many nations.
documents.text: “American patriotism is not of soil; we are not aborigines, nor of ancestry, for we are of all nations; but it is essentially personal enfranchisement, for ‘where liberty dwells,’ said Franklin, the sage of the Revolution, ‘there is my country.’”

documents.title: Women's proper sphere
documents.source: Catharine Beecher, A Treatise on Domestic Economy (1841). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A best-selling advice book telling middle-class women that their place was the home.
documents.text: “In this Country, it is established, both by opinion and by practice, that women have an equal interest in all social and civil concerns. . . . But in order to secure her the more firmly in all these privileges, it is decided, that in the domestic relation, she take a subordinate station.”

documents.title: A visitor sees the mills
documents.source: Charles Dickens, American Notes (1842). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An English novelist's account of a visit to Lowell, written for readers in Britain.
documents.text: “These girls, as I have said, were all well dressed. . . . They were healthy in appearance, many of them remarkably so, and had the manners and deportment of young women: not of degraded brutes of burden.” Dickens also noted that in July 1841, no fewer than 978 of the girls were depositors in the Lowell Savings Bank.

documents.title: Unions declared lawful
documents.source: Commonwealth v. Hunt, Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, 1842, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The court's decision in a case charging a union of shoemakers with criminal conspiracy.
documents.text: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decided in 1842 that unions were lawful organizations as long as they used legal means, including striking, to achieve their goals. A union was not a criminal conspiracy simply because its members acted together.

documents.title: Famine brings a new workforce
documents.source: Immigration figures from the Statistical Abstract of the United States. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Official arrival figures for the year the Irish potato famine struck hardest.
documents.text: In 1847, the year the potato famine struck hardest, 234,968 immigrants arrived in the United States, nearly half of them Irish. Four-fifths of Irish immigrants settled in the port cities of the Northeast, where many took mill work and canal and railroad work for lower wages than the farm daughters they replaced.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the market revolution changed workers' lives, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the cutoff of British goods during the Embargo and the War of 1812, or the growth of a national market after 1815.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the limits of the change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Panic of 1837, the putting-out system, or the free-labor ideology.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where workers' lives changed and where older ways persisted.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The market revolution changed workers' lives to a great extent: it moved work from the home to the factory, paid it in cash wages, and drew immigrants and farm daughters into a new kind of working life, but it left most workers poor, and its gains were uneven.
Context: Before 1800, most Americans farmed for their families and made goods at home. The Embargo Act of 1807 and the War of 1812 cut off British goods, and after the war, mills, canals, and wage work spread.
Grouping: Documents 1, 2, and 5 show the new mill workforce and its strikes; Documents 3 and 7 show immigration feeding the workforce; Documents 4 and 6 show the limits on women and the legal standing of unions.
Beyond the documents: The putting-out system survived in some trades, and the free-labor ideology promised wage earners a rise to independence that most never reached; the Panic of 1837 undercut the Lowell strikes.
Complexity: The change was deep but uneven: farm daughters won cash wages and savings, yet ended as a passing workforce, while immigrants won work at lower wages, and women were told their place was the home.
